analysis.one_liner: Bars ticketing companies from locking venues into exclusive contracts lasting more than a few years.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2023 and received no hearing, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tell the Federal Trade Commission to stop ticket companies from signing exclusive contracts with venues that last too long. Today, one dominant ticketing company can lock up a stadium or arena for years at a time, so fans who want a ticket to a show at that venue have to buy through that one company. The bill would have the FTC write rules declaring contracts longer than a set period (at least four years) illegal, and let the FTC fine companies that break the rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Concertgoers, sports fans, and theater audiences, who would get more than one choice of where and how to buy tickets, and potentially better prices and fees as ticketing companies compete for venues. Performing artists would also gain leverage, since long exclusive contracts are a key part of the dominance they complained about.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits primary ticketing providers from holding exclusive contracts to sell tickets for all or substantially all events at a venue when the contract runs for an 'excessive duration' set by FTC rule, and that minimum period must be more than four years.

The FTC would enforce the ban as an unfair method of competition under the FTC Act, with civil penalties capped at the volume of commerce affected, and regular antitrust laws would still fully apply on top of it.
It applies to large venues (audience capacity of at least 5,000), which covers the major arenas, stadiums, and theaters where exclusive ticketing deals matter most.

It was introduced in April 2023, in the wake of public outrage when fans could not get tickets to a major 2022 tour sold through one dominant ticketing platform; Klobuchar and Blumenthal, both antitrust-focused senators, sponsored it.

analysis.who_pays: The dominant ticketing company, which would lose the long-term exclusive contracts that guarantee it the initial sale of tickets at major venues, and the venues themselves, which currently receive large guaranteed payments in exchange for signing multi-year exclusivity deals and would have less to bargain with if contracts had to be shorter.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dominant ticketing company and large venues

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban exclusive contracts outright: it only bans contracts longer than a period the FTC defines, and that period must be more than four years, so shorter exclusives (and up to at least four years) would stay legal.

Venues negotiate large up-front payments and investment in exchange for long-term exclusivity; shorter contracts could mean less guaranteed money for arenas and possibly for the events and ticket prices they support.
The whole remedy depends on the FTC writing and enforcing rules, so its practical effect would depend on which administration runs the FTC and how aggressively it polices ticketing.

Critics of exclusive-deal limits argue exclusivity can benefit fans too, since a single provider can invest in venue infrastructure and reliability; the bill assumes competition in ticketing outweighs those efficiencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For fans, the upside is real but incremental: more competition at the ticket window, which historically means lower service fees and fewer outright sell-outs caused by one platform's failures. The costs fall on the ticketing giant and on venues' guaranteed contract revenue, not on ticket buyers. The bill is narrow by design — it does not break up any company or ban exclusivity outright — which makes it hard to argue the costs to the public are serious, but it also means it only loosens the problem rather than solving it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2023, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 26, 2023 by Senator Klobuchar with Senator Blumenthal, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote appears in the action history through the end of the 118th Congress.
The bill's one cosponsor was Senator Blumenthal of Connecticut, one of 48 Senate Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant ticketing company keeps its long-term exclusive venue contracts, and large venues keep the guaranteed payments those contracts bring. Nothing changed for fans waiting in line on one platform.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The dominant ticketing company and its venue partners

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator (MN), bill sponsor and chair of the Judiciary Competition subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on April 26, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only additional senator to sign on.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or vote in the year and a half after referral.

against.name: Live Nation Entertainment (Ticketmaster)
against.what_they_did: The company whose long-term exclusive venue contracts were the bill's target; it publicly defended its exclusive contracts as pro-competitive and lobbied against measures to open up ticketing.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown exists; the bill's only two Senate supporters were both Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Primary ticketing companies (the Ticketmaster/Live Nation model)
industries.note: The bill strikes at the company's core strategy: signing venues to long exclusive contracts so every initial ticket sale runs through it. Fans pay for that lock-up through high service fees and a lack of alternatives when one platform fails. The bill would force those contracts to be shorter and expose the ticketing giant to FTC penalties and existing antitrust law.

industries.industry: Large concert and sports venues (5,000+ capacity)
industries.note: Venues currently trade long-term exclusivity for large guaranteed payments and infrastructure investment; the bill would cut those deals shorter. They would gain the freedom to switch or split ticketing providers, which benefits their customers, but lose guaranteed revenue.
